\subsection{Complete-source and receiving-history controls}
\label{app:state-completeness}

\paragraph{Population and protocol.}
The additional Qwen3-8B/MedCalc study uses a frozen $124$-question pool
from $14$ calculator skills, selected using historical outcomes before
these interventions. No item is removed based on the new repair outcome.
The correct-skill donor answers $121/124$ correctly; the no-skill baseline
answers $4/124$. Wrong uses the original unrelated skill; Neutral uses a
predeclared unrelated natural-language document, not a guarantee of zero
influence. Source positions and prompt lengths are aligned. The protocol
uses BF16, eager attention, split prefill, greedy decoding and a $1536$
new-token limit. All $49$ conditions per item share this protocol.
Fresh screening for a correct donor and incorrect Wrong and no-skill
baselines retains $114$ questions, reproducing the earlier $L16$
$S/C/SC$ accuracies of $3.5/7.0/42.1\%$. Table~\ref{tab:state-completeness}
instead reports all $124$ items, including donor and receiver errors.

\paragraph{Source coverage and receiving history.}
Before continuation, $SC$ source K/V matches the donor elementwise at all
$36$ layers for both receivers and $L\in\{8,16,24\}$. A further explicit
all-layer source write leaves all $744$ paired generated token sequences
unchanged. Other prefix K/V need not match the donor and can vary with
intervention depth. Copying only those other positions gives $3/124$
and $10/124$ correct answers (Wrong/Neutral); copying the complete prefix
cache gives $121/124$ in both contexts and reproduces all donor tokens
($248/248$ pairs). This is a positive control using same-question donor
computation. Replacing all source KV and replaying the prompt after the
skill gives $120/124$ in both contexts. Only $48/124$ outputs per context
are token-identical to the donor, so replay is not an exact numerical
identity under BF16 and different prefill computation shapes.

\paragraph{Paired uncertainty and truncation.}
The $SC@8-SC@24$ accuracy difference is $66.1$ percentage points in Wrong
and $64.5$ in Neutral. Resampling whole skill groups with replacement
$10{,}000$ times gives exploratory $95\%$ percentile intervals of
$[49.3,78.5]$ and $[40.5,82.8]$ points. The signs are positive/tied/negative
in $12/2/0$ and $11/2/1$ of the $14$ groups, respectively.
No $SC@8$ output reaches the token cap; $SC@24$ has three capped outputs
in Wrong and none in Neutral. Assigning capped outcomes adversarially
against the difference still leaves gaps of $63.7$ and $64.5$ points.
These intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The small
number of groups and single model/task limit extrapolation.

\paragraph{Cache content and layer windows.}
Holding all-layer source coverage fixed, correct-skill KV yields
$29.8/25.0\%$ accuracy in Wrong/Neutral, versus $4.8/6.5\%$ for
unrelated-skill KV and $1.6/4.0\%$ for a second predeclared neutral
text's KV. The Wrong-to-Wrong source write is also a token-exact identity
control. Four equally sized eight-layer source writes, at layers
$0$--$7$, $8$--$15$, $16$--$23$ and $24$--$31$, yield
$3.2/3.2/1.6/4.0\%$ in Wrong and $0.8/4.0/4.8/5.6\%$ in Neutral.
These windows individually recover little; comparison with all $36$
layers does not identify the minimum required coverage because the write
budgets differ. Late $SC$ need not improve on $C_{\mathrm{all}}$:
at $L24$ in Wrong, accuracy is $25.8\%$ versus $29.8\%$.

\paragraph{Audit and scope.}
All $6076$ formal records and $14$ implementation-check records passed
full key-set, identity, source-write and file-hash checks. An independent
process regraded answers, with identical labels in forward and reverse
order. Cache-coverage claims use saved runtime elementwise checks, not
an offline re-execution of the model. The study does not repeat the full
transfer/knockout depth sweep, identify a unique semantic variable in
other-position caches, or validate the margin sufficient condition.

The complete-source controls further motivate testing which parts of
the receiving history must be recomputed, and whether the required budget
can be predicted on held-out skills. Extending these controls beyond

\paragraph{Is complete source state sufficient?}
We test this on a fixed pool of $124$ Qwen3-8B/MedCalc questions from
$14$ skills, using both an unrelated-skill receiver and a fixed unrelated
text receiver (Neutral). All conditions share BF16, eager attention,
split prefill and greedy decoding. This pool retains fresh donor failures;
it differs from the $114$-item repair screen above.
For $SC$ at $L8$, $L16$ and $L24$, every source-position K/V tensor at
every layer exactly matches the donor before continuation. Explicitly
rewriting all source layers changes none of the $744$ paired outputs.
Yet accuracy drops from $91.9\%$ to $25.8\%$ between $L8$ and $L24$
in the unrelated-skill receiver, and from $91.1\%$ to $26.6\%$ in Neutral
(Table~\ref{tab:state-completeness}). Thus missing source-cache layers
alone cannot account for the late deficit.

Copying the complete prefix cache reproduces the donor tokens on every
question in both contexts. Copying source KV and recomputing the prompt
positions after the skill instead reaches $96.8\%$, although its tokens
match the donor on only $48/124$ questions per context. The remaining
state therefore matters: caches at question and template positions can
retain consequences of earlier skill processing. These controls establish
neither a minimal state to copy nor a low-cost reuse method.
Appendix~\ref{app:state-completeness} gives content and layer-window
controls, paired uncertainty estimates and implementation checks.
